Puzzle 4 · 5 of 10

One frame, from tree to pixels

Puzzles 0 to 3 ended with an up-to-date tree of UI elements. A tree isn't pixels yet. Here's what Compose does with it in every frame, in three steps, and why a parent sizes each child only once.

  • Puzzle 3: What gets skipped

    A call is skipped when every argument equals the one stored in its slots last time. Stable types (Int, String, a data class of vals) are compared with equals. Unstable types (a class with a var, a List) are compared by instance with ===, under strong skipping, on by default since Kotlin 2.0.20. So a new list built on every run makes its child run every time; keep it in remember, or in state, and the same instance comes back.

The problem

Puzzle 1 said some calls leave a node, a real UI element, and puzzles 2 and 3 showed how the tree of nodes stays up to date. But a Column node holding a Text and a card says nothing yet about pixels: how wide is the text, where does the card start, and what puts the colour on the screen? Something has to turn the tree into a picture, again for every frame that changes.

See it

The building block

A frame (one redraw of the screen) is made in three phases, always in this order. Android's docs give them as: composition, "what UI to show"; layout, "where to place UI"; drawing, "how it renders". Composition is everything puzzles 0 to 3 covered: run what's marked, skip what's equal, update the nodes.

Layout walks the node tree from the top. A parent hands each child constraints: the smallest and largest width and height the child may take. The parent then asks each child to measure itself: the child picks a size within the constraints, after measuring its own children the same way. A Text with too little width wraps onto more lines and gets taller; it can't get wider than its constraints allow. With the children's sizes known, the parent picks its own size.

A parent may measure each child only once per layout. The reason is depth: if every parent measured its children twice, each level down would double the work, and a tree ten levels deep would cost a thousand times more. With one measure per child, layout visits each node once.

Then placement: the parent sets each measured child's x and y, relative to itself. The Column puts the Text at the top and the card under it, at y = 40, the height of the Text.

Drawing comes last. Each node paints itself, at its place, onto a canvas: the drawing surface, with commands such as drawRect (fill a rectangle with a colour) or draw a line of text. Compose's Canvas is a Kotlin interface. On Android, the object behind it wraps Android's own canvas; on iOS, it wraps Skia's (the KMP course, puzzle 15). Your composables never see which one.

All three phases run, in principle, for every frame, but each one is skipped where its inputs didn't change: a frame where only a colour changed can redo drawing alone. Puzzle 2's state reads are noted per phase too, and puzzle 7 uses that to move work out of composition.

Go deeperWho decides a size: the parent or the child?
A parent passes constraints with a minimum and maximum width of 340 pixels, and the child, a Text, would like 120. What size does it get?

340 wide. When the smallest and largest allowed widths are the same, the child has no choice; that's how a modifier like fillMaxWidth works. The child still chooses its height within its own height constraints.

Back to the main puzzle

The analogy

The theatre once more. The script says who is in the scene (composition). Before the curtain, the stage manager tells each group how much of the stage it may use, each performer says how much room they need within that, and the stage manager marks each one's spot on the floor with tape (layout). Then the lights come up and the scene is painted onto the stage (drawing). Nobody asks a performer twice for their size: with dozens of groups inside groups, the rehearsal would never end.

Check yourself

A Column gets at most 300 pixels of width. Its child, a Text, needs 400 pixels to fit its words on one line. What happens when the Text is measured?

Not quite. A child picks its size within the constraints; it can't choose more than the maximum.

Right. Within the constraints, so it wraps.

Not quite. Each child is measured once per layout; the constraints come first. Re-read that part ↑

Why may a parent measure each of its children only once per layout?

Right. One measure per child keeps layout linear in the tree.

Not quite. Sizes come from the layout phase, not from slots.

Not quite. Measuring picks a size; drawing is a later phase.

A card's text changes from one short line to a three-line paragraph. Which phases have new work to do?

Not quite. The card got taller, so it must be measured again and what's below it moves.

Right. A size change reaches every phase.

Not quite. Each frame needs layout and drawing again for whatever changed size or looks. Re-read that part ↑

Sources
  • Android Developers: Jetpack Compose phases ("Compose has three main phases: Composition: What UI to show. Compose runs composable functions and creates a description of your UI. Layout: Where to place UI. This phase consists of two steps: measurement and placement."; "Drawing: How it renders. UI elements draw into a Canvas, usually a device screen."; "Conceptually, each of these phases happens for every frame; however to optimize performance, Compose avoids repeating work that would compute the same results from the same inputs in all of these phases."; "Note that each node was visited only once."; "In contrast, if each node was visited multiple times, the traversal time increases exponentially.")
  • Android Developers: Custom layouts ("Parents define the constraints for their child elements."; "An element is asked to define its size within those constraints."; "Compose UI does not permit multi-pass measurement."; "This means that a layout element may not measure any of its children more than once in order to try different measurement configurations.")
  • Compose foundation source: Size.kt (fillMaxWidth makes the content fill the incoming maximum width "by setting the [minimum width][Constraints.minWidth] and the [maximum width][Constraints.maxWidth] to be equal to the [maximum width][Constraints.maxWidth] multiplied by [fraction]")
  • Compose UI source: Canvas.kt (public interface Canvas {, with public fun drawRect(left: Float, top: Float, right: Float, bottom: Float, paint: Paint))
  • Compose Multiplatform source: Canvas.skiko.kt (actual typealias NativeCanvas = SkCanvas, imported as org.jetbrains.skia.Canvas; and on Android, AndroidCanvas.android.kt: public actual typealias NativeCanvas = android.graphics.Canvas)

What you now know

Compose makes a frame in three phases, always in this order. Composition runs what's marked and updates the tree of nodes. Layout passes constraints down, measures each child once within them, lets each parent pick its own size, then places each child relative to its parent. Drawing has each node paint itself onto a canvas. Each phase can be skipped when its inputs didn't change.
